A 50-line page produces ~12–50MB of transient allocations, and a typical multi-act scan (dozens of pages) sums to hundreds of MB–GB of churn on the import thread, causing repeated GC stalls on top of the already ~95ms compute per line. The code already shows this class of allocation sensitivity was recognized for the DFS stack (336-341), but the hottest inner loop is unpooled. Fix: reuse a per-thread scratch IntArray and FloatArray sized to the max rec crop (48×1024) and clear/rewrite them per crop (they are consumed synchronously by the ONNX run), and reuse a single tall scaled bitmap for all boxes of a page. {performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] android/app/src/main/kotlin/com/tiltastech/lineguide/PaddleOcrPlugin.kt:309-328,437-438,470-488 — per-text-line FloatArray/IntArray allocation churn inside the recognition loop — each OCR job issues one `imageToTensor` per detected line: `scaleBitmap` + `IntArray(w*h)` + `FloatArray(3*w*h)`, plus a second `FloatArray(buf.remaining())` copy in `run` (line 499); with recMaxWidth=1024 and recHeight=48 that is ~590KB per line. A 100-page script at ~50 lines/page = 5,000 iterations ≈ 3GB of heap churn per import, adding GC pauses to an already compute-bound multi-minute job and stalling the app when the GC runs. Reachable by any user importing their own PDF. — pool/reuse per-thread buffers scoped to the job (the capture is sequential on one worker thread) instead of allocating fresh arrays per crop, and read the ONNX output into a reusable buffer rather than a fresh FloatArray. {mlx-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [low] android/app/src/main/kotlin/com/tiltastech/lineguide/PaddleOcrPlugin.kt:429-437 — per-crop/per-page tensor allocation churn in the OCR hot loop: recognize() allocates `IntArray(w*h)` + `FloatArray(3*w*h)` + two tiny `mean/std` arrays per text line (imageToTensor, lines 470-484), and detection allocates a ~960×960×3 FloatArray plus IntArray per page (line 295). Scale: ~40 lines/page × ~40 pages in a script import ≈ 1.2 GB+ churn plus ~15 MB/page for detection — on a memory-constrained device (Galaxy A35-class) this forces repeated GC pauses during a job that already runs seconds per page. The compute dominates (~95 ms/line), so impact is secondary but real. Fix: reuse a single `IntArray`/`FloatArray` sized to `recHeight×recMaxWidth` (every crop fits within bounds) and hoist `mean`/`std` to static fields; size the det buffer once per page. {kotlin-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

A corrupt or unsupported page loses its text in the import while the Dart side sees a clean result, and because no `FlutterError`/`NOT_IMPLEMENTED` is raised, the documented ML Kit fallback (which only triggers on an error) is bypassed — surface per-page inference failures as errors so the caller can fall back, instead of returning empty lines. {ml-inference-pipeline-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [low] ios/Runner/PaddleOcrPlugin.swift:202 — synchronous `NSLog` with string interpolation per page inside the ocrPdf loop — trigger: once per page for every PDF import; consequence: each call is a synchronous formatted write (plus the per-page timing Date arithmetic), minor but avoidable serial cost on the OCR queue; fix: switch to `Logger`/`OSSignposter` intervals, or gate the per-page log behind a debug flag. {ios-performance-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}
- [high] ios/Runner/PaddleOcrPlugin.swift:251 — `try? run(...)` swallows ONNX inference failures into an empty `[]` lines/blocks result, so a model/tensor failure on any page is indistinguishable from a genuinely blank page and the Flutter importer silently imports an empty page (silent content loss on the OCR-dependent import path; no ML-Kit fallback since `ready` stays true). Same root cause at the recognition call (line 338) and the model-load error path at line 120 (`try? String(contentsOfFile: keysPath)` → `keys=[] ` yet `ready=true`, so OCR emits unusable blank/space text instead of falling back). — Fix: propagate the underlying error (rethrow to the `do`/`handle` error path or return a typed FlutterError) and keep `ready = false` when the keys dictionary fails to load, so the caller can fall back to ML Kit. {swift-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [low] ios/Runner/PaddleOcrPlugin.swift:251,338 — `try? run(...)` swallows the model-error (throws), which surfaces as an empty OCR result instead of a failure — a corrupt/incompatible model yields "no text detected" rather than an error the Dart side can report; a silent data-loss path for the transcript — capture the error and return a per-page failure marker (or a FlutterError) instead of empty blocks. {maintainability-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] ios/Runner/PaddleOcrPlugin.swift:258 (recognize at :331, imageToTensor at :388, run at :410) — recognition of every detected text box is a separate synchronous ORT session run, each allocating a fresh crop tensor (imageToTensor allocates a UInt8 draw buffer + 3×w×h Float array), a fresh NSMutableData/ORTValue, and a fresh output Float array; boxes are never batched, so a page with N lines pays N× fixed ONNX run/dispatch overhead and N× buffer allocation — authenticated user importing an OCR'd script (hundreds of pages × tens of boxes/page = tens of thousands of sequential runs) sees import wall-clock scale linearly with total line count rather than amortized per page — smallest safe fix: concatenate all box crops into one batched rec input and issue a single rec run per page (PP-OCRv6 rec accepts arbitrary batch), reusing the tensor/NSMutableData buffers across boxes {mlx-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

Fix: hoist the offsets to a `static let` constant (or two `[Int]`/`[Int]` arrays) above the loops, or unroll the four neighbor pushes. {ios-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

- [medium] lib/data/services/recording_sync_service.dart:553 — `getCachedRecordings` performs a synchronous `File.existsSync` per cached entry on the calling (UI) isolate, and `launchRecordingSync` (context: production_providers.dart:470,485) invokes it on every production open and once more after each full sync. The global `_cache` is never evicted (only manual clear), so with even ~1–2k cached recordings (a few productions' worth of lines; each entry is a blocking filesystem stat on the main thread, plus a map of allocations per entry) the production-open path stalls for tens of ms and grows linearly with total cached recordings across all productions. Observable: visible lag entering a production / on sync completion as the cache grows. Smallest safe fix: batch existence checks asynchronously (pooled `File.exists`) or drop the per-entry stat and let playback surface a missing file per line instead of pre-filtering every entry. {dart-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] lib/data/services/recording_sync_service.dart:553 — getCachedRecordings scans the entire global `_cache` (keyed only by lineId, line 125) and runs a synchronous `File.existsSync` per entry on the UI isolate; it is invoked twice per production open from the launch future (production_providers.dart:469-472, 483-487) plus after every full sync. Trigger frequency: every production open; growing input: total cached recordings across all productions, which is unbounded (see next finding); work per unit: one map iteration + one blocking stat per entry for every entry, regardless of the requested production. Consequence: tens of ms of frame jank on the main isolate for a mature cache, worsening with lifetime footprint because there is no per-production index. Fix: keep a per-production map (`Map<productionId, Map<lineId, cached>>`) so the scan touches only the requested production's entries, and/or move the stat pass onto a compute isolate. {metal-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] lib/data/services/recording_sync_service.dart:553-575 — `getCachedRecordings(productionId)` performs a synchronous `File.existsSync()` on every entry of the GLOBAL cache (all productions, not just the requested one) on the main isolate, and is called twice per production open plus after each sync (production_providers.dart:470, 485; context file). Frequency: once or twice on every production open and at sync completion; work scales O(total cached recordings across all productions), each stat blocking the UI thread. With a cast that has collected a few hundred castmate takes, each open stalls for hundreds of ms of sync filesystem stats on the UI isolate — worse for users in many productions because the cache map is global. Smallest safe fix: do the existence check asynchronously (`await File.exists()` in an already-async path), or validate lazily only for entries a consumer actually reads/plays, keeping the deleted-file re-download contract by checking the file at playback/sync-decision time instead of enumerating the whole cache. {mlx-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] lib/data/services/recording_sync_service.dart:553-575 — the recording cache is global and never evicted (only cleared via clearCache/clearAllCaches), and every production open triggers up to three O(cache) `File.existsSync()` passes on the UI isolate: `getCachedRecordings` at production_providers.dart:470, `syncForProduction`'s hydration, and `getCachedRecordings` again at production_providers.dart:485 (per entry, lines 562, 404, 413). Because the cache is keyed globally across ALL productions ever opened, the per-open stall grows without bound (each entry = one filesystem stat, ~µs-10µs each, so a 3-5k-entry lifetime cache adds tens of ms of main-thread work on every open, plus unbounded disk growth). Each manifest write (190-200, 461, debounced for realtime at 650) also re-encodes the whole global cache on the UI isolate. Fix: evict with an LRU/cap when the cache or disk exceeds a bound, partition the index per production so sync/manifest only touch the active production's entries, and defer the existsSync sweep to the sync worker instead of the open path. {flutter-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

- [high] lib/features/home/home_screen.dart:438-460 — `_ensureScriptLoaded` awaits `loadPersistedScript` and then unconditionally assigns `currentScriptProvider` without re-checking that `production` is still the current production (the same guard `_reconcileCloudScript` applies at lines 282 and 337 is missing here) — a user who opens a menu action on production A and quickly taps into production B gets A's in-memory script under B: the editor/cast screens show the wrong script, and a subsequent editor mutation (`scheduleScriptPersist` path) would persist and cloud-push A's lines under B's production id — silent cross-production script corruption — re-check `ref.read(currentProductionProvider)?.id == production.id` after the await before setting the state. {observability-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}

Reachable by any authenticated user via the card overflow menu (lines 409-425). - [high] lib/features/home/home_screen.dart:450-458 — `_ensureScriptLoaded` (and the same pattern in `_openProduction` at 229-240) awaits a persisted-script read and then writes `currentScriptProvider` without re-checking that `currentProductionProvider` is still the production it loaded for, unlike the guarded `_reconcileCloudScript` (which re-checks at line 282 precisely because "the user can open another production while this is in flight"). - [medium] lib/features/script_editor/script_editor_screen.dart:503,925 (same class lib/features/script_import/ocr_review_screen.dart:363,693) — every `PdfPageView` embed is keyed on the per-line id (`'editor-src-${line.id}'`, `'editor-sheet-${current.id}'`, `'sheet-${current.id}'`, `'src-${selected.id}'`), so each step in the low-OCR walk-through (Prev/Next/Remove/Looks right), and each tablet line selection, destroys the widget and recreates it with empty state: the PDF is reopened+re-parsed (`_doc?.dispose()` then `openFile`), the page is re-rendered (multi-MB RGBA), and the per-instance `_pageCache`/`_pageOcrCache` (pdf_page_view.dart:59-60,69) are discarded — so the native single-page OCR (~1 s per pdf_page_view.dart:21) re-runs for the SAME source page each time. Flagged lines cluster 2-5+ per scanned page, so a 20-flagged-line cleanup session or a tablet scan pays ~1-2 s per step and tens of MB of transient RGBA allocations where same-page steps should be instant once the page cache hits — reachable by any user reviewing/editing their own imported script. Fix: key the viewer on `(pdfPath, pageNumber)` (e.g. `ValueKey('sheet-p${line.sourcePage}')`) so the instance and its caches survive same-page steps, and from `didUpdateWidget` call `_locateHighlight` when only `highlightText` changed — the cached page OCR then serves subsequent same-page steps. {flutter-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

Fix: capture only the final drop position and persist through the debounced save path (`scheduleScriptSave`) used by every other edit, or debounce `persistScript` to the last entry of a drag gesture. {dart-performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

- [low] scripts/verify-apk-ort.sh:12-15 — under `set -euo pipefail`, `find … | head -1` (line 12) and `grep -E … | head -1` (lines 14 and 15) SIGPIPE the producer whenever more than one line matches, so the assignment fails and set -e kills the script with no diagnostic — the verify step dies silently mid-check in CI, indistinguishable from a crashed runner — replace `grep … | head -1` with `grep -m1` and capture the find output fully before selecting (or append `|| true` to the head pipelines) {maintainability-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}

- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260314061409_initial_schema.sql:133-135 — `recordings` UPDATE policy checks only `auth.uid() = user_id` with no WITH CHECK on `production_id`, and it survives the lockdown — an authenticated member can repoint their own recording row's `production_id`/`line_id` into any other production, polluting another tenant's recording feed with bogus takes (the policy alone gates only "row is mine") — fix: add `with check (auth.uid() = user_id and public.is_production_member(production_id, auth.uid()))`. {maintainability-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260314061409_initial_schema.sql:133-135 — recordings UPDATE policy checks only `auth.uid() = user_id` with no membership or production constraint (and no later migration hardens it — 20260703140000 item 11 fixes only INSERT), and WITH CHECK defaults to USING so `production_id`/`audio_url`/`line_id` are freely editable — a user can repoint their own row at a production they don't belong to, planting an attacker-chosen recording entry visible to that production's cast (cross-tenant write; requires knowing the target production UUID, hence not high) — add `public.is_production_member(production_id, auth.uid())` to the update's WITH CHECK. {dependency-audit@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}
- [low] supabase/migrations/20260314120000_add_script_lines.sql:16-17/45 and supabase/migrations/20260813100000_add_script_scenes.sql:25/44-46 — explicit `idx_script_lines_production`/`idx_script_scenes_production` duplicate the index already created by the `unique (production_id, order_index)` constraints on the same two columns. Trigger: every insert/update of script_lines and script_scenes (organizer sync writes each line). Consequence: each write maintains two identical indexes, doubling index-maintenance cost and WAL on the most churned tables, with zero read benefit. Smallest safe fix: drop the explicit indexes and rely on the unique-constraint index; if the constraint must later be dropped, re-add the index then. {performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260314120000_add_script_lines.sql:48 and supabase/migrations/20260314061409_initial_schema.sql:141 — script_lines and recordings are published on supabase_realtime; supabase-realtime emits one WAL event per changed row. Assumption: cloud sync writes script lines one row at a time (the 20260701090000 comment describes per-line round-trips). Trigger: organizer pushes a full script revision; each of N line inserts/updates + recordings broadcasts to every subscribed client. Growing input: N (lines per play, unbounded thousands) × M (connected cast). Consequence: a single full-script sync fires O(N×M) WebSocket broadcasts, saturating realtime fan-out and client handling during every edit burst. Smallest safe fix: batch the push in one transaction and emit a single "revision changed" event clients use to re-pull, or drop the tables from the publication. {performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260314140000_fix_rls_recursion.sql:7-14 (helper), 38-40/53-56/76-82 (policies), and supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:37-46/57-79 — `is_production_member`/`is_production_organizer` are SECURITY DEFINER, so the planner cannot inline/correlate the EXISTS; every RLS-candidate row on productions, cast_members, script_lines, recordings, and storage.objects executes one function call (an index probe on cast_members each). Trigger: any authenticated member read/sync of a production script, recordings list, or cast list; the storage policies add a per-object plpgsql `storage.foldername(name)`+uuid-cast (with exception handler). Growing input: script length and recording count per production are unbounded (a full play's transcript is thousands of lines). Work per unit: 1 helper execution × candidate row. Impact: fetching a ~5–10k-line script pays ~5–10k non-inlinable function invocations on top of the row scan, latency grows linearly with lines/recordings per production and doubles when the storage plpgsql path is hit; exacerbates connection/latency on every sync. Smallest safe fix: rewrite policies as plain correlated subqueries (e.g. `exists (select 1 from cast_members cm where cm.production_id = script_lines.production_id and cm.user_id = auth.uid())`) so they inline onto idx_cast_members_production_user, or convert the helpers to SECURITY INVOKER with pinned `search_path` to allow inlining. {performance-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260315_cast_join_code.sql:6 — one migration mixes ACCESS-EXCLUSIVE DDL (`ADD COLUMN ... UNIQUE` index build at :6, whole-table backfill UPDATE at :9-11, `SET NOT NULL` full scan at :14) on the live `productions` table with no `lock_timeout` — reads and writes to productions stall for the combined index build + scan + backfill duration, and queue behind any long query — split into add-nullable → batched backfill → NOT VALID check → SET NOT NULL, with `SET LOCAL lock_timeout` at the top. {sql-migration-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}

- [high] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141 — the SECURITY DEFINER join-flow RPCs (`join_production` here, `fetch_cast_for_join` here at :166, and `claim_cast_invitation` in 20260319000001:54) authorize on the production UUID alone — none verify the caller knows the join code, is an invited user, or is a member — so any authenticated user who holds a production UUID (it travels in recording object paths, debug reports, or leaked invite links; and the lockdown itself says UUIDs are no longer enumerable, so secrecy is the only barrier) can call `fetch_cast_for_join` to list the cast, then `join_production`/`claim_cast_invitation` to become a member and read the full script, every castmate recording, and cast contact info — a cross-tenant disclosure that section 5 of this migration's own comment claims to have closed but explicitly defers ("Requiring the join code itself … tracked separately") — fix: require the production's `join_code` as an argument to `join_production`/`claim_cast_invitation` and verify it against `productions.join_code` (and bind `claim_cast_invitation` to the intended invitee), and gate `fetch_cast_for_join` on membership. {dependency-audit@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [high] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141 — the rewritten `join_production` (and sibling `claim_cast_invitation`, 20260319000001_join_flow_rpc_v2.sql:54) is SECURITY DEFINER and gates only on the caller knowing a production/cast-member UUID — it never verifies the join code or any invitation; any authenticated user who learns a UUID (leaked by a member, stored in a recording object path, or obtained via the brute-force above) self-joins and gains full script and recording access to another organizer's production — require the join code to be presented and verified inside the RPC (the file itself notes this as tracked debt at lines 139-140, but the hole is live today). {db-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}
- [high] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141 — the rewritten `join_production` RPC still lets **any authenticated user** self-join **any** production by raw UUID (`prod_id::uuid`, line 157) with no join-code check, and it is SECURITY DEFINER so the tightened RLS policies don't apply. A user who knows one production UUID (shared by a castmate, or learned previously) can join it, then read the full script and download every recording via the member policies; `fetch_cast_for_join` (line 166) likewise returns the cast list and membership ids for an arbitrary prod_id, and `claim_cast_invitation` (20260319000001:54) lets the caller claim every open invitation in that production without ever presenting the code. The migration's own comment (line 139) acknowledges the code check is deferred, but the hole shipped: this defeats the "enumeration closed" claim because possession of a single UUID bypasses the code entirely — add a `join_code` parameter to `join_production`/`claim_cast_invitation` and verify it against `productions.join_code` before inserting. {db-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141-162 — `join_production` still lets any authenticated user self-join any production by UUID with no join-code verification (the comment at :139-140 defers this); production UUIDs leak through recording storage object paths (`<productionId>/<character>/<line>.m4a`) and prior membership records, so a user who obtains a UUID of a production they don't (or no longer) belong to can join and then read the full script and download every castmate recording — fix the class: require and verify `join_code` inside the SECURITY DEFINER RPC (new signature, as the comment tracks). {maintainability-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

- [low] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:107 — fetch_cast_for_join returns cm.user_id for every cast member, disclosing existing members' auth account UUIDs (account↔character correlation) to any prospective joiner holding the join code — null out user_id for members the caller hasn't joined as, and only expose the full id on rows the caller is eligible to claim. {linux-server-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:107 — `fetch_cast_for_join` returns the full cast_members roster (member `id`, `user_id`, names) to any authenticated caller who presents the production's join code (or is a member): the code is shared with all invited participants, so a leaked/guessed code turns this SECURITY DEFINER function into a roster-and-claimable-ids dump that feeds `claim_cast_invitation` (line 147) ID-based takeover — consequence: every production UUID plus its invitee `user_id`s becomes enumerable to anyone holding a code — scope the projection (drop `user_id` and member `id` for non-members; only return claimable member ids to the authenticated caller after an ownership check), and move the join flow off a broad `select *`-style dump behind one clickable code. {db-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:113,143,165 — new SECURITY DEFINER functions get EXECUTE granted to PUBLIC by default in Postgres; only `lookup_production_by_join_code` is revoked from anon at line 81, so `fetch_cast_for_join`, `join_production`, and `claim_cast_invitation` remain callable by anon — an unauthenticated caller with a valid (prod_id, code) pair gets the full roster (line 101-110) with no account and no rate limit, contradicting the stated intent at lines 79-80 — add `revoke execute on function ... from public, anon` for each new function. {db-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}
- [high] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:131 — the rate limit added in §1 is applied only to lookup_production_by_join_code (line 70); the other three code-accepting functions (join_production lines 131-136, fetch_cast_for_join lines 95-100, claim_cast_invitation lines 154-162) treat the join code as an oracle without calling check_join_rate_limit — a wrong code raises 'Invalid join code for this production' and a right one succeeds, so any authenticated user can brute-force 6-char codes (~887M) at full speed, defeating the anti-guessing control the migration itself introduces — call check_join_rate_limit() in each code-consuming function (same budget as lookup), or route every code check through the throttled path. {linux-server-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:131 — the 20-lookups/5-min rate limit (lines 37–59) is only invoked by `lookup_production_by_join_code`; the three other code-verification paths — `fetch_cast_for_join` (lines 95–100), `join_production` (lines 131–136), and `claim_cast_invitation` (lines 159–162) — check `join_code` with no throttle — an authenticated user who learns a production UUID (share links, existing members) can brute-force the 6-char code through `join_production` at full speed, defeating the exact threat section 1 says it mitigates — call `perform public.check_join_rate_limit();` (or extract a shared `verify_join_code` helper that includes it) at the top of each of the three functions. {sql-migration-review@deepinfra-zai-org-glm-5.3-flash}

- [low] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:137 — `join_production` inserts a `cast_members` row unconditionally with no "already a member" guard, so a code-knowing authenticated user can rejoin repeatedly and mint duplicate roster rows with arbitrary `character_name`/`display_name`; whether a unique `(production_id, user_id)` constraint exists was not confirmed in this batch (requested context unavailable) — add an `is_production_member` check or upsert before inserting, or verify the existing unique constraint. {sql-migration-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}

- [high] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:154 — claim_cast_invitation still lets any holder of the production's join code claim any row where user_id IS NULL: the new check only binds the claim to the production's code, not to the intended invitee (the row stores no invitee identity), and fetch_cast_for_join (line 107) hands out those unclaimed row ids to any code holder — an authenticated user who obtains the shared/printed join code can enumerate unclaimed seats and take one, displacing the invited actor (the same invitation-takeover class the migration claims to fix) — store a per-invitee token (or the invitee's auth identity) on the unclaimed row and verify it in the claim, and stop exposing unclaimed rows in fetch. {linux-server-review@deepinfra-deepseek-ai-deepseek-v4-flash-0731}
